title: Please, don't, and go ahead — commands at three levels
title_target: सीधे जाइए, फिर बाएँ मुड़िए — siidhe jaaiye, phir baaeⁿ muRiye
goal: Ask, tell and forbid in the right tone — and find your way when you're lost, which in India always means asking people, not looking at a map.
bekal: addressing strangers with the right title

dialogs.title: संवाद — Lost in the lanes
dialogs.intro: Ani is looking for a mosque and asks a passerby. Notice that almost every sentence the man says is a command — and not one of them sounds bossy.

lines.speaker: आनी:
lines.id: Excuse me, sir. Where is the mosque?
lines.literal: brother — sir, sorry — do. mosque — where — is?

lines.speaker: राहगीर:
lines.id: The mosque? Go straight, then turn left.
lines.literal: mosque? straight — go, then — left — turn.

lines.speaker: राहगीर:
lines.id: Five minutes on foot. Don't rush, the sun is strong.
lines.literal: five — minutes, on-foot. hurry — don't — do, sunshine — sharp — is.

lines.speaker: आनी:
lines.id: Thank you. And at the crossroads?

lines.speaker: राहगीर:
lines.id: Don't turn at the crossroads. Just keep going straight.
lines.literal: crossroads(obl.) — at — don't — turn. straight — walking(fem.) — keep-on.

lines.speaker: आनी:
lines.id: Got it. Thank you very much.

lines.speaker: राहगीर:
lines.id: Child, one thing — keep your bag in front. It's crowded.
lines.literal: daughter, one — thing — bag — front — keep. crowd — is.

lines.speaker: आनी:
lines.id: Yes, thank you. You're very kind.
lines.literal: ji, thanks. you — very — kind — are.

lines.speaker: राहगीर:
lines.id: It's nothing. If you get lost, just ask anyone.
lines.literal: some — thing — not. way — forget — then — someone(obl.) — from — ask — take.

notes: **Polite commands are formed with -इए, and "please" is already built in.** Drop -ना from the dictionary form and add **-इए**: जाना → **जाइए**, बैठना → **बैठिए**, बोलना → **बोलिए**, रुकना → **रुकिए**. ⚠️ This form is **not rude at all** — it's the normal way to ask something of someone you respect. Adding कृपया actually makes it sound like an official announcement.

**Five verbs with irregular commands, all of them common.** करना → **कीजिए**, देना → **दीजिए**, लेना → **लीजिए**, पीना → **पीजिए**, होना → **होइए**. Learn all five now; you'll use them every day, especially दीजिए and कीजिए.

**Forbidding uses मत, not नहीं.** *मत जाइए* (don't go), *जल्दी **मत** कीजिए* (don't rush), *यहाँ **मत** बैठो* (don't sit here). ⚠️ नहीं negates statements (*मैं नहीं जाती* — I don't go), while मत forbids actions. There's also the gentler, slightly pleading **न**: *न जाइए* sounds like "please don't go…".

**Three levels, and as a visitor you only need one.** **आप** → -इए (जाइए) for everyone. **तुम** → -ओ (जाओ) for close friends and children. **तू** → the bare stem (जा) for very close friends, or in anger. ⚠️ Using the तुम form with an auto driver or a waiter **sounds condescending**, even if you mean to be friendly. Use -इए with everyone, no exceptions; nobody is offended by too much respect.

**Two ways to soften even more.** **ज़रा** ("a little") goes in front: *ज़रा रुकिए* (wait a moment, please), *ज़रा सुनिए* (excuse me, a moment) — the latter is the most natural way to get a stranger's attention. And the tail **-गा**: *आइए* (come, now) → *आइएगा* (do come again, sometime). The -इएगा form sounds very friendly and a little warm.

**Addressing strangers: pick a title, not a bare "you".** **भाई साहब** for a grown man, **बहन जी** or **मैडम** for a grown woman, **भैया** for a young man who serves you (driver, vendor, waiter), **दीदी** for a young woman, **अंकल जी / आंटी जी** for older people. ⚠️ Calling out just *सुनिए!* with no title sounds cold; adding a title changes the whole tone.

**ख़ुदा हाफ़िज़ — the Muslim goodbye.** It means "may God protect you", and another form you'll hear is **अल्लाह हाफ़िज़**. In India you'll hear greetings from several religions all day long: **नमस्ते**, **आदाब**, **सत श्री अकाल**, **जय श्री कृष्ण**. When in doubt, you can answer any of them with **नमस्ते**, and no one will be offended.

grammars.title: Commands at three levels
after: ⚠️ The last row introduces something you'll hear a lot: **two verbs in a row**, the second coloring the first. *पूछ लीजिए* = "just ask (for yourself)", *बता दीजिए* = "just tell (me)". These are compound verbs; they don't change the meaning, only the tone. You don't need to form them yourself yet — just recognize them, and don't be thrown when you hear two verbs side by side.

grammars.title: Directions
after: ⚠️ **पता means both "address" and "knowledge".** *आपका पता क्या है?* = what's your address? But *मुझे पता नहीं* = I don't know — a sentence you'll use several times a day.

sections.title: Asking the way, and ten emergency phrases

blocks.text: In India, asking people is almost always faster than a map — and people will stop, think about it, and explain carefully. One warning: some people don't like to disappoint you by saying "I don't know", so ask two different people if the directions sound unsure.

blocks.title: Three phrases that rescue beginners most often
items: **फिर से बोलिए।** — "Please say it again." Don't hesitate to use it three times in a row. Indians are used to repeating, and repeating usually means slowing down too.
**मुझे हिंदी थोड़ी थोड़ी आती है।** — "I know a little Hindi." Said at the start of a conversation, it changes how fast the other person talks for the rest of it.
**यह हिंदी में क्या कहते हैं?** — "What's this called in Hindi?" While pointing. It's not just a survival tool; it's the fastest way to learn anyone has ever found.

blocks.text: ⚠️ One fair word about safety. The man's advice in line eight of the dialogue — *बैग सामने रखिए* — is advice Indians really do give visitors in crowded places, and accepting it is a sign not of suspicion but of respect. In crowds, big markets and train carriages, carrying your bag in front is ordinary practice for everyone, locals and guests alike.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in the right order.

items: Excuse me, where is the station?

answers: जाइए — बैठिए — कीजिए — दीजिए — सुनिए — लीजिए
सीधे जाइए, फिर बाएँ मुड़िए। — मस्जिद कहाँ है? — जल्दी मत कीजिए। — कितनी दूर है? — फिर से बोलिए।
ज़रा सुनिए, स्टेशन कहाँ है? — सीधे जाइए, फिर दाएँ मुड़िए। — कितनी दूर है? — थोड़ा धीरे बोलिए। — मुझे पता नहीं। — वहाँ मत जाइए।
